name: Voltaire Statue (Square Honoré-Champion)
short_description: Stone replacement statue of the philosopher Voltaire by Léon-Ernest Drivier, installed in 1962 to replace the original 1885 bronze on Quai Malaquais that was melted down by the Nazis in 1941.

_pipeline.address: Square Honoré-Champion, 1 rue de Seine, 75006 Paris
_pipeline.discovery_notes: Commemorates Voltaire near Quai Voltaire where he died in 1778; the original 1885 bronze was a Third Republic monument and the current Drivier statue was reinstalled in June 2024 after restoration.

name: Rue de Rivoli
short_description: Long arcaded thoroughfare decreed by Napoleon in 1801 and named for his 1797 victory at the Battle of Rivoli, running along the Louvre and Tuileries.

_pipeline.address: Rue de Rivoli, 75001/75004 Paris (1st and 4th arrondissements)
_pipeline.discovery_notes: One of Paris's most famous shopping and ceremonial streets, running from Place de la Concorde to the Marais and lined with Percier-and-Fontaine arcades.

name: Place des Pyramides
short_description: Square at Rue de Rivoli holding Emmanuel Frémiet's 1874 gilded equestrian statue of Joan of Arc, near the spot where she was wounded in her 1429 attempt to take Paris.

_pipeline.address: Place des Pyramides, Rue de Rivoli, 75001 Paris
discovery_sources: Un Jour de Plus à Paris
_pipeline.discovery_notes: Royalist and Catholic pilgrimage point centred on the gilded Joan of Arc statue; popular Instagram spot just off Rue de Rivoli at the Tuileries.

name: Quartier de l'Horloge
short_description: Modernist 1970s redevelopment north of the Pompidou Centre, named for Jacques Monestier's 1979 bronze automaton clock 'Le Défenseur du Temps' on Rue Bernard de Clairvaux.

_pipeline.discovery_notes: The four-metre brass automaton clock fights a rooster, crab and dragon hourly — a quirky kinetic sculpture restored in 2022–23 after years of silence.

name: Rue Charles V
short_description: Quiet Marais street named for Charles V, who in the 14th century moved his royal residence to the nearby Hôtel Saint-Pol and triggered the district's transformation from marsh to noble quarter.

_pipeline.discovery_notes: Backstreet of the southern Marais lined with discreet 17th-century hôtels particuliers; useful axis between Place des Vosges and the Bastille area.

name: Rue de Lappe
short_description: Working-class Bastille street that became the heartland of the bal-musette accordion-dance scene from 1900, home to Balajo and once over a dozen rowdy dance halls.

_pipeline.discovery_notes: Auvergnat immigrants brought the cabrette and accordion here; Brassaï photographed its smoky bals in the 1930s and Balajo still operates at no. 9.

name: Fouquet's
short_description: Red-awninged brasserie founded by Louis Fouquet in 1899, listed as a French historical monument since 1990 and host of the annual post-César Awards dinner.

_pipeline.discovery_notes: Long-time hangout of French film and political elites at the corner of Champs-Élysées and Avenue George V; iconic Parisian power-lunch venue.

name: Rimbaud Statue (Sully Morland)
short_description: Bronze 'L'Homme aux semelles devant' by Jean-Robert Ipoustéguy, inaugurated in 1984 at Place du Père-Teilhard-de-Chardin, its title a pun on Rimbaud's nickname 'man with soles of wind'.
name_variations: L'Homme aux semelles de vent (nickname source)

_pipeline.address: Place du Père-Teilhard-de-Chardin, near Boulevard Henri-IV, 75004 Paris (statue relocated in 2018 to the Musée de la Sculpture en Plein Air at Port Saint-Bernard / Square Tino-Rossi, 75005 Paris)
_pipeline.discovery_notes: One of the few public sculptures of Rimbaud in Paris; the wind-pun pose makes it a literary-tour anchor near Sully-Morland metro.

name: Église Saint-Pierre de Montmartre
short_description: Romanesque-Gothic church begun in 1133 and consecrated by Pope Eugenius III in 1147, the surviving sanctuary of the destroyed Montmartre Abbey and one of the oldest churches in Paris.

_pipeline.discovery_notes: Hidden behind Sacré-Cœur on the western flank of the butte and often missed by tourists despite being effectively the second oldest church in Paris.

name: Lapin Agile
short_description: Surviving Montmartre cabaret on the slope behind Sacré-Cœur, taking its name from André Gill's 1875 painted sign of a rabbit leaping from a saucepan and immortalized by Picasso's 1905 painting.

_pipeline.discovery_notes: Picasso, Modigliani, Apollinaire and Utrillo all drank here during the Bohemian heyday; still operating nightly chanson cabaret.

name: Musée Nissim de Camondo
short_description: Petit-Trianon-inspired mansion built 1911–14 by Count Moïse de Camondo to display 18th-century French furniture, bequeathed in memory of his son killed in WWI and family later murdered at Auschwitz.

_pipeline.discovery_notes: Frozen-in-time hôtel particulier whose family tragedy is one of the most poignant Jewish-Parisian stories; closed for renovation, scheduled to reopen 2026.

name: Musée Jacquemart-André
short_description: Second Empire mansion built 1869–1875 by architect Henri Parent for banker Édouard André and painter Nélie Jacquemart, opened as a museum in 1913 with their Italian Renaissance and 18th-century French collection.

_pipeline.discovery_notes: Combines a lavishly preserved aristocratic interior with a small but exceptional Italian Renaissance gallery — a stronger candidate than larger museums for art-lover off-trail tours.

name: Passage Poncelet
short_description: Small 17th-arrondissement passage running between 27 Rue Poncelet and 12 Rue Laugier, named for mathematician Jean-Victor Poncelet and adjacent to the famed Marché Poncelet open-air market.

_pipeline.address: Passage Poncelet (27 Rue Poncelet to 12 Rue Laugier), 75017 Paris
_pipeline.discovery_notes: Quiet pedestrian passage at the heart of the Ternes food-shopping district; pairs naturally with the celebrated Rue Poncelet market for a 17e gastronomy stop.
